messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Reyes is a 24-year-old Colombian American QA engineer who presented for an initial evaluation approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic gas explosion at a crowded downtown food hall where he had been eating lunch with two coworkers. The blast, later attributed to a ruptured commercial gas line that city inspectors had reportedly flagged but not acted upon, killed four people and injured dozens more. Mateo was seated near the back of the building when the explosion tore through the kitchen area. In the chaos that followed, he found his coworker Miguel pinned beneath a collapsed ceiling partition, conscious and calling out for help. Mateo attempted to lift the debris but could not move it, and within minutes emergency responders arrived and redirected him outside. Miguel survived but sustained serious injuries requiring months of hospitalization. A second coworker, a woman named Daniela who had been closer to the blast, did not survive. Mateo walked out of the building with minor lacerations and no broken bones, a fact that has never felt like luck to him.

In the weeks following the explosion, Mateo returned to his job at a mid-sized software company, where he works remotely from a small apartment he shares with no one. The work itself — running systematic tests to find what breaks, what fails, what was overlooked — had once suited his careful, methodical temperament. Now the irony felt almost punishing. He had come to believe, with a quiet certainty that resisted any counter-argument, that he had failed Daniela and Miguel in the most fundamental way a person can fail another. He had been right there. He had tried and it had not been enough, and in his accounting, not being enough and failing were the same thing.

The rumination settled into a particular groove: he found himself returning again and again to the specific sequence of choices that morning — why he had suggested that food hall, why he had picked that table, what would have happened if they had left ten minutes earlier. These thoughts were not fleeting. They occupied long stretches of his evenings, the kind of thinking that feels like work but produces nothing. He had come to understand his own future through the same lens: nothing good could follow from this, not for him. The explosion had not simply happened to him; it had revealed something about the shape of his life going forward.

His avoidance organized itself around the edges of what reminded him. He stopped watching television almost entirely — the news cycle in the months following the disaster had been saturated with coverage of infrastructure failures, industrial accidents, and safety violations, and even a brief headline crossing his peripheral vision was enough to pull him toward a feeling he struggled to name, a loosening of the boundary between himself and the room, a sense of unreality that frightened him more than straightforward fear would have. When a colleague mentioned a car pileup during a video call, Mateo went quiet for the remainder of the meeting and spent the next hour unable to concentrate on his test scripts. He began keeping his camera off during team standups, and then began missing them altogether, citing connection issues. His manager has raised the pattern twice now.

He has also gone out of his way to avoid any encounter with police. The officers at the scene that day had been the ones to redirect him away from Miguel, and though he understood intellectually that they were doing their jobs, the sight of a uniform now carried the full weight of that moment — the moment he stopped trying. He reroutes his occasional errands to avoid the precinct two blocks from his building.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation: the missed meetings, the evenings lost to counterfactual loops, a growing sense that he had become someone he did not recognize. He had come to believe that the world was genuinely unpredictable in a malevolent way — that harm could arrive from any direction and that no amount of care or vigilance would be sufficient. He arrived at intake quiet and precise in his language, describing his symptoms with the same systematic thoroughness he brings to his work. What he said he most feared was that the person he had been before the explosion — someone who believed good things were still possible — was simply gone.
